TikTok Project¶

Dinh Manh Tuan - November 2025

This project is a case study in the Google Advanced Data Analytics Certificate on Coursera. The objective is to classify whether a post on TikTok is whether a claim or an opinion video based on extracted features. To do this, we use a dataset provided by Google with more than 19000 records to use for our Logistic Regression and Machine Learning models

The skill I acquired included:

  • Python programming,
  • Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), data visualization (seaborn, matplotlib)
  • Statistical testing,
  • Regression model building,
  • Machine Learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost).

Data Dictionary¶

Table 1. Tiktok Dataset Dictionary

Column name Type Description
# int TikTok assigned number for the video with claim/opinion.
claim_status object Whether the published video is identified as an opinion or claim. An opinion refers to an individual's or group’s personal belief or thought. A claim refers to information that is unsourced or from an unverified source.
video_id int Random identifying number assigned to the video upon publication on TikTok.
video_duration_sec int The duration of the published video in seconds.
video_transcription_text object Transcribed text of the words spoken in the video.
verified_status object Indicates whether the TikTok user who published the video is verified or not verified.
author_ban_status object Indicates the user’s permission status: active, under scrutiny, or banned.
video_view_count float The number of times the video has been viewed.
video_like_count float The number of times the video has been liked by other users.
video_share_count float The number of times the video has been shared by other users.
video_download_count float The number of times the video has been downloaded by users.

Investigate outliers of the dataset

In this dataset, we can define outliers of a distribution as values that are above 1.5 interquartile range:

In [18]:
count_cols = ['video_view_count',
              'video_like_count',
              'video_share_count',
              'video_download_count',
              'video_comment_count',
              ]

for column in count_cols:
    q1 = data[column].quantile(0.25)
    q3 = data[column].quantile(0.75)
    iqr = q3 - q1
    median = data[column].median()
    outlier_threshold = median + 1.5*iqr

    # Count the number of values that exceed the outlier threshold
    outlier_count = (data[column] > outlier_threshold).sum()
    print(f'Number of outliers, {column}:', outlier_count)

2. Hypothesis testing¶

Let's take a look into the video view count of videos posted by verified and unverified users:

In [19]:
data.groupby(['verified_status'])['video_view_count'].describe()
Out[19]:
count mean std min 25% 50% 75% max
verified_status
not verified 17884.0 265663.785339 325681.881915 20.0 5160.00 46723.0 523099.50 999817.0
verified 1200.0 91439.164167 221138.764926 37.0 2974.75 6023.5 9036.75 997769.0

We can notice a clear difference in descriptive statistics between the two groups; unverified accounts produce more videos (17884 vs 1200), and their average view count is much higher than verified users. And verified users show a large spread i counts, given that the maximum count is not so different between two groups (~1M). This raises a questions:

Are videos posted by verified users statistically differet in mean view count from those posted by unverified users?

Descriptive statistics alone cannot confirm whether the differences we observe are meaningful or simply due to sampling variability. Therefore, we turn to formal statistical hypothesis testing.

  • Null hypothesis: There is no difference in the mean number of views between TikTok videos posted by verified accounts and TikTok videos posted by unverified accounts (any observed difference in the sample data is due to chance or sampling variability).
  • Alternative hypothesis: There is a difference inthe mean number of views between TikTok videos posted by verified accounts and TikTok videos posted by unverified accounts (any observed difference in the sample data is due to an actual difference in the corresponding population means).

Therefore, we construct a two-sample t-test, choosing the significance level = 5%.

In [20]:
# Save each sample in a variable
not_verified = data[data["verified_status"] == "not verified"]["video_view_count"]
verified = data[data["verified_status"] == "verified"]["video_view_count"]

# Implement a t-test using the two samples
result = stats.ttest_ind(a=not_verified, b=verified, equal_var=False)
result
Out[20]:
TtestResult(statistic=25.499441780633777, pvalue=2.6088823687177823e-120, df=1571.163074387424)

Since the p-value is extremely small (much smaller than the significance level of 5%), we reject the null hypothesis. We can conclude that there is a statistically significant difference in the mean video view count between verified and unverified accounts on TikTok. Nevertheless this case, Tiktok view counts distribution is heavily right-skewed, with several extreme viral videos creating fat tails. To further ensure our conclusions are not driven purely by these extreme outliers, we can apply a robustness check by using a non-parametric Mann-Whitney U (median shift) method:

In [21]:
# Robustness check
stats.mannwhitneyu(not_verified, verified, alternative="two-sided")
Out[21]:
MannwhitneyuResult(statistic=14477078.5, pvalue=1.9312984413553236e-91)

Both the parametric two-sample t-test and the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test consistently lead to the same conclusion: videos posted by verified TikTok users receive significantly fewer views on average than videos posted by unverified users.

Taken together, these results suggest that the observed gap in view counts is systematic rather than random, and likely reflects underlying behvioral or structural differences between two groups of users. For example:

  • Unverified accounts may post more sensational or clickbait-style content that attracts higher view counts.
  • Verified accounts may consist of established organizations or public figures whose content is more informational or moderated.
  • Platform dynamics or algorithmic factors may unintentionally amplify certain types of unverified accounts.s?

The next step will be to build a regression model on verified_status. A regression model is the natural next step because the end goal is to make predictions on claim status. A regression model for verified_status can help analyze user behavior in this group of verified users. Technical note to prepare regression model: because the data is skewed, and there is a significant difference in account types, it will be key to build a logistic regression model.

In [25]:
# Use resampling to create class balance in the outcome variable, if needed

# Identify data points from majority and minority classes
data_majority = data[data["verified_status"] == "not verified"]
data_minority = data[data["verified_status"] == "verified"]

# Upsample the minority class (which is "verified")
data_minority_upsampled = resample(data_minority,
                                 replace=True,                 # to sample with replacement
                                 n_samples=len(data_majority), # to match majority class
                                 random_state=0)               # to create reproducible results

# Combine majority class with upsampled minority class
data_upsampled = pd.concat([data_majority, data_minority_upsampled]).reset_index(drop=True)

One of the model assumptions for logistic regression is no severe multicollinearity among the features. The above heatmap shows that the following pair of variables is strongly correlated: video_view_count and video_like_count (0.86 correlation coefficient).s. To build a logistic regression model that meets this assumptionI willld exclu e video_like_cou.tAmong the variables that quantify video metrics, I retainep video_view_count, video_share_count, video_download_count, and video_comment_count as features.

Construct the model¶

In [30]:
# Select outcome variable
y = data_upsampled["verified_status"]

# Select features

# Compute values for confusion matrix
log_cm = confusion_matrix(y_test_final, y_pred, labels=log_clf.classes_)

# Create display of confusion matrix
log_disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=log_cm, display_labels=log_clf.classes_)

# Plot confusion matrix
log_disp.plot()

# Display plot
plt.show()

The upper-left quadrant displays the number of true negatives: the number of videos posted by unverified accounts that the model accurately classified as so.

The upper-right quadrant displays the number of false positives: the number of videos posted by unverified accounts that the model misclassified as posted by verified accounts.

The lower-left quadrant displays the number of false negatives: the number of videos posted by verified accounts that the model misclassified as posted by unverified accounts.

The lower-right quadrant displays the number of true positives: the number of videos posted by verified accounts that the model accurately classified as so.

A perfect model would yield all true negatives and true positives, and no false negatives or false positives.

Create classification report for logistic regression model¶

In [56]:
# Create classification report
target_labels = ["verified", "not verified"]
print(classification_report(y_test_final, y_pred, target_names=target_labels))

              precision    recall  f1-score   support

    verified       0.74      0.52      0.61      4459
not verified       0.63      0.82      0.71      4483

    accuracy                           0.67      8942
   macro avg       0.69      0.67      0.66      8942
weighted avg       0.69      0.67      0.66      8942

The classification report above shows that the logistic regression model achieved a precision of 61% and a recall of 84%, and it achieved an accuracy of 65%. Note that the precision and recall scores are taken from the "not verified" row of the output because that is the target class that we are most interested in predicting. The "verified" class has its own precision/recall metrics, and the weighted average represents the combined metrics for both classes of the target variable.

4. Build Machine Learning Models¶

Step-by-step action plan:¶

Use the training/validation/test split (60/20/20) to build a reliable workflow.

Perform feature engineering to select the most predictive variables.

Train multiple models and select the best based on validation performance, focusing on F1 score.

Choose the random forest model, as recommended by the Data Science Lead, for its interpretability and strong performance.

Finalize the model on the test set and prepare an executive summary including:

Key metrics (F1, precision, recall)

Feature importance

Confidence in model accuracy

Ethical considerations and stakeholder impact

Recommend whether the model is suitable for production and suggest safeguards (e.g. human review for edge cases).

Modeling workflow and model selection process

Previous work with this data has revealed that there are ~20,000 videos in the sample. This is sufficient to conduct a rigorous model validation workflow, broken into the following steps:

  1. Split the data into train/validation/test sets (60/20/20)
  2. Fit models and tune hyperparameters on the training set
  3. Perform final model selection on the validation set
  4. Assess the champion model's performance on the test set

We have to import the data and process them again for the new ML model

In [58]:
data = pd.read_csv('tiktok_dataset.csv')

data.dropna(inplace = True)

data.loc[data['video_like_count'] > upper_limit, 'video_like_count'] = upper_limit
In [60]:

data.loc[data['video_comment_count'] > upper_limit, 'video_comment_count'] = upper_limit

Build a Random Forest model¶

In [70]:
# Instantiate the random forest classifier
rf = RFC(random_state = 0)
# Create a dictionary of hyperparameters to tune
cv_params = {'max_depth': [3,4,5, None],
             'min_samples_leaf': [1,2,3],
             'min_samples_split': [2,3,4],
             'max_features': [2,3,4],
             'n_estimators': [75, 100, 150]}
# Define a list of scoring metrics to capture
scoring = {
    'f1': 'f1',
    'recall': 'recall',
    'accuracy': 'accuracy',
    'precision': 'precision'
}

# Instantiate the GridSearchCV object
rf_cv = GridSearchCV(rf, param_grid = cv_params, cv = custom_split, scoring = scoring, refit = 'recall')

High Recall (1.0) The model is correctly identifying all actual claims in the validation set. This is crucial in a claims classification context, where missing a true claim (false negative) could lead to moderation failures or inappropriate content staying online.

High Precision (0.990) Out of all the predictions labeled as claims, 99% are actually claims. This means the model is not labeling random videos as claims, avoiding false positives that could waste moderators’ time..3f}')

The most predictive features were video_share_count and video_view_count, followed by video_download_count and video_comment_count. This suggests that user engagement metrics are highly indicative of whether a video contains a claim. The results are not surprising, as content that generates more interaction is more likely to include assertive or controversial statements.

5. Conclusion¶

To conclude, this projectct applied an end-to-end data analytics and machine learning pipeline to understand content behavior on TikTok and to predict whether a video is classified as a claim or an opinion. Starting from exploratory data analysis, we identified strong skewness, heavy tails, and substantial heterogeneity in engagement metrics such as views, likes, shares, and downloads. These observations motivated careful feature engineering, robustness checks, and the use of models capable of capturing non-linear relationships rather than relying solely on classical statistical assumptions.

Through hypothesis testing, we established that verified and unverified users exhibit statistically significant differences in engagement patterns, particularly in video view counts. This result provided both behavioral insight and empirical justification for incorporating account-level attributes—such as verified_status and author_ban_status—into predictive models. The robustness checks using non-parametric tests ensured that our conclusions were not driven by extreme viral outliers, reinforcing the reliability of the analytical foundation before moving into machine learning.

Building on this foundation, Decision Tree and XGBoost models were employed to classify claim status. These models proved especially suitable due to their ability to handle skewed data, interaction effects, and complex feature dependencies. Feature importance analysis revealed that engagement-related variables (views, shares, likes) and account attributes play a dominant role in classification performance, highlighting how behavioral signals can be leveraged to distinguish potentially misleading content from opinion-based videos. In particular, tree-based models provided both strong predictive performance and interpretability, allowing us to identify which features most influence model decisions.

Overall, this project demonstrates how combining EDA, statistical testing, feature engineering, and machine learning can produce both actionable insights and robust predictive systems. The results underscore the importance of feature-driven modeling in content moderation tasks and suggest that interpretable ML models like Decision Trees and XGBoost can serve as powerful tools for supporting trust, safety, and responsible AI deployment on social media platforms. king.
